episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, September eleventh, two thousand twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.
<break time="1.0s"/>

First, in Practical Tips, Harvard College Dean David Deming wants students to show more than a polished final paper. He wants colleges to make their thinking visible through drafts, discussion, revision, presentations, and peer review.

In a September ninth Chronicle interview, Deming rejects unenforceable A.I. bans while defending the value of students' own writing. One example begins with a student-written first draft, followed by a conversation with the professor and a revised second draft. A.I. can provide feedback, but the student still has to create the work, explain the choices, and respond to questions. Deming also points to oral presentations and peer review as ways to make academic work more communal and accountable. These are his proposals, not a new Harvard-wide policy.

His larger argument reaches beyond writing rules. If A.I. makes some forms of expertise more abundant, Deming argues that colleges can place greater value on what people learn with and from one another: how to explain an idea, persuade an audience, negotiate disagreement, and earn trust.

That leads to a better assignment-design question than simply asking whether A.I. is allowed: What can this student explain and defend without the tool? When that answer is clear, A.I. can support the work without becoming the only evidence that learning occurred.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Next, in Case Study, Texas A&M is finding that the most important part of an A.I. role-play may not be the avatar. It may be the instructional design behind the conversation.

A September eighth EDUCAUSE Review case study describes how Mays Business School and Dell Technologies built an A.I.-avatar platform for interviews, sales conversations, presentations, and coaching. The article was published in collaboration with Dell, an EDUCAUSE Mission Partner. Students enter through the learning management system and complete either A.I.-avatar or face-to-face role plays. The platform can capture recordings, transcripts, and performance data, then support feedback from instructors, peers, role players, and a trained A.I. system.

Initial pilots generated hundreds of practice sessions. But the revealing finding came as faculty refined the experience. General prompts and broad rubrics produced weaker feedback. Detailed scenarios, defined roles, staged conversations, and explicit criteria made the practice more realistic and the response more useful. Texas A&M is still establishing the key performance indicators that will show what the approach changes over time.

For another college, the place to begin is not the avatar. Begin with the conversation students will practice, the decisions they will make, and the evidence that will show whether they improved. A.I. can multiply the practice, but faculty design determines whether the practice is worth repeating.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Practical Tips, the University of San Diego offers a way to replace one blanket A.I. rule with assignment-level decisions. Its Learning Design Center is implementing the A.I. Assessment Scale to connect permitted A.I. use with the purpose of the work.

A.I.A.S. two point one organizes assignments into five levels: No A.I., A.I. Planning, A.I. Collaboration, Full A.I., and A.I. Exploration. A controlled exam might require independent work. A collaborative assignment might allow A.I. for drafting or feedback while requiring students to evaluate, modify, and integrate what the system produces. The level changes because the learning goal changes.

The useful move is a three-part sequence. Name the learning objective, choose the role A.I. may play, and specify the evidence students will provide. A source-evaluation assignment, for example, could permit planning help while requiring students to document their checks, revisions, and final judgment.

USD says more guides and examples are coming. Faculty can use the central idea now. Start with what students are supposed to learn, then make the A.I. rule serve that purpose instead of allowing the technology to define the assignment.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Insights and Trends, Austin Community College is asking whether a student alert can lead somewhere useful. Its Digital Twin Initiative is designed to shorten the distance between a warning and help a student can actually use, according to a September eleventh Inside Higher Ed report.

ACC plans to combine information from multiple systems into a broader student view, then connect students with advising, tutoring, financial aid, mental-health, and basic-needs resources. The initial version is rolling out to roughly forty-six thousand active credit students this fall, with more features planned for spring.

Chancellor Russell Lowery-Hart offered a simple example: a grade could be followed by tutoring options that show available times. A planned adviser dashboard would give staff a broader view as the multiphase system develops. The rollout is early, so the report does not yet offer retention results.

The design question is not whether a college can generate another alert. It is whether the alert reaches the right person, triggers a clear next step, and gives the student a realistic option at the moment help is needed. That is where predictive technology becomes student support rather than another dashboard.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Returning to Practical Tips, Dartmouth is pairing permission to use A.I. with work that other people can challenge. Writing in The Atlantic on September fifth, President Sian Leah Beilock argues against blanket bans and proposes that every undergraduate complete a team A.I. project before graduation, while preserving room for faculty to require A.I.-free work. It is an ambition, not a Dartmouth mandate.

A concrete graduate example is already taking shape at Dartmouth's Tuck School of Business. Its M.B.A. First-Year Project added an A.I. requirement that asks students to research, build, and test tools for real clients. Tuck describes a nine-week cycle with required primary research and weekly meetings with clients and faculty.

The value is not simply that students receive permission to use A.I. They have to investigate a consequential problem, explain their choices, test what they build, and respond when a client or professor challenges the result. The work leaves a trail of decisions that can be questioned and improved.

For faculty adapting a client project, three decisions matter: what the client can challenge, what students will verify, and how they will respond when the tool gives an unusable answer. A.I. becomes part of the learning when students remain responsible for the judgment.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Back in Insights and Trends, MIT is addressing a familiar faculty problem. A generic A.I. workshop can explain the technology and still leave educators wondering how it belongs in their discipline. MIT News reports that a July pilot brought nineteen educators from seven institutions together to adapt A.I. and machine-learning materials for their classrooms.

The structure behind the pilot is more useful than the event itself. MIT's course pairs a six-unit common module on machine-learning foundations with a six-unit disciplinary module that applies those ideas to fields such as sustainability, molecular biology, and finance. The catalog emphasizes framing problems, choosing methods, and evaluating results.

That creates two deliberate handoffs. First, learners develop a shared technical language. Then the discipline changes the cases, evidence, and standards of judgment. MIT's version lists calculus and programming prerequisites, so a program serving beginners would need a different entry point. The pilot does not yet report adoption or learning results at the participating institutions.

For curriculum leaders, the transferable idea is architectural: decide what every learner needs in common, then let each field rebuild the application around questions it recognizes. A.I. literacy becomes more meaningful when it has somewhere disciplinary to go.
<break time="1.0s"/>

Finally, in Beyond Ed, NASA and IBM have released an open A.I. model built to help researchers work across the Moon's many kinds of scientific data. NASA announced the Lunar Foundation Model on September tenth as one of the first open-source A.I. models designed specifically for lunar science.

The model card describes a vision-transformer system trained on roughly two million aligned lunar tile bundles. Those bundles bring together eleven data types at one-meter and one-hundred-meter scales. Demonstrated research tasks include crater mapping, identifying irregular mare patches, and estimating where polar ice may be more likely.

The model weights, benchmarks, and fine-tuning resources are openly available under an Apache two point zero license. Researchers still have to interpret the outputs carefully. An ice-prospectivity map is not a direct measurement of ice, and NASA has not validated the model for landing-site selection or hazard clearance.

The higher-education connection is the research model it offers universities. A campus team can inspect the system, test it against benchmarks, adapt it to a new question, and contribute findings from the same shared foundation. This is A.I. not as an answer machine, but as reusable scientific infrastructure.
<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's most relevant A.I. and innovation news for higher ed, covering the week ending September eleventh, two thousand twenty-six. Thanks for listening.

quickHits.reviewNotes: The USD page and AIAS 2.1 framework were checked. The USD page is undated, describes implementation in progress, and reports no local outcome evidence. The framework is an assignment-design tool, not an AI detector.

quickHits.headline: NASA and IBM Turn Moon Data Into Open AI Research Infrastructure
quickHits.summary:
Most AI headlines still revolve around chatbots. Demonstrated research tasks include crater mapping, identifying irregular mare patches, and estimating where polar ice may be more likely.

The model weights, benchmarks, and fine-tuning resources are openly available under an Apache 2.0 license. Researchers still have to interpret the outputs carefully: an ice-prospectivity map is not a direct measurement of ice, and NASA has not validated the model for landing-site selection or hazard clearance.

What makes this a Beyond Ed story is the research model it offers universities. A campus team can inspect the system, test it against benchmarks, adapt it to a new question, and contribute findings from the same shared foundation. quickHits.reviewNotes: NASA's announcement, the NASA-IBM model card, and the public repository were checked. Roughly two million bundles, 11 modalities, two scales, and demonstrated tasks come from the model card. Outputs are not calibrated predictions, ice prospectivity is not measured ice, and the model is not validated for operational landing or hazard decisions. The repository says pretraining code is not included.
